sources.title: LaVerle Berry, Historical Setting, in Libya: A Country Study (1989)
sources.note: Library of Congress country study, research completed 1987. Printed pages 18 to 24; direct PDF read, local copy in first sub-bundle. Used for broad administrative phases and Italian invasion, not uncritical descriptions of Bedouin culture.

sources.title: Xavier de Planhol, Éléments ottomans dans la physionomie géographique de la Cyrénaïque (1975)
sources.note: Original geographic field research undertaken in November 1974, published pages 353 to 363. Full indexed abstract and page 354 read. Separates mobile tribal administration from permanent posts.

sources.title: Fredrick Walter Lorenz, The Second Egypt (2021)
sources.note: Original research using Ottoman archives; full shared article read. Ottoman-Sanusi Alliance and European Threat section supports lodge networks and exports; later Cretan settlement is not projected into the imported interval.

sources.title: Ahmet Kavas, Senûsî, Muhammed b. Ali (2009)
sources.note: TDV scholarly biography read in full. Childhood instruction by paternal aunt Fatima, Bayda lodge in 1843, Jaghbub library and works list. Implausible mass-conversion totals in this article are not used.

sources.title: James Hamilton, Wanderings in North Africa (1856)
sources.note: Original account of 1852 journey, directly read. Explicit foreign observer with colonial and religious prejudices; selected concrete descriptions only. Pages 5 to 7, 117 and 121.

sources.title: National Library of Israel, Kitab al-masa’il al-ashr, Cairo edition 1353 AH
sources.note: Primary library catalog of Muhammad ibn Ali al-Sanusi book, Arabic title and edition information directly read. Catalog dates Cairo Matbaat al-Maahid edition 1353 AH, corresponding to 1934/35. Sample reproduces the cataloged Arabic title, not an autograph image.

sources.title: Jean-Marie Lassère, Syphax, Encyclopédie berbère 43 (2019)
sources.note: Original scholarly article, pages 7655 to 7660. Publisher challenge; full author text read through https://www.researchgate.net/publication/396090825_Syphax_S93 . Printed publication is 2019, not search engine 2018. Used paragraphs 1 to 4, 9 and 12. Some mistaken personal names in paragraph 11 are not repeated.

sources.title: Livy, History of Rome, book 24, chapters 48 to 49
sources.note: Ancient Roman narrative in English translation, directly read on university site. Roman characterization of Numidians is not adopted as neutral fact.

sources.title: Appian, Spanish Wars, sections 29 to 30
sources.note: Ancient narrative in Horace White translation; full indexed passage read. Banquet is explicitly presented as Appian’s account, not a reconstructed ordinary household meal.

sources.title: Georges Vuillemot, Siga et son port fluvial (1971)
sources.note: Original excavation report, Antiquités africaines 5, pages 39 to 86. Full indexed page 77 read; direct access failed. Hellenistic occupation spans third and second centuries into first century BCE, and particular rooms cannot securely be labeled homes or stores. OCR final paragraph incorrectly renders the earlier fifth/sixth centuries as CE; that passage is not used.

sources.title: Gabriel Camps, Beni Rhénane (1991)
sources.note: Scholarly archaeological account, original paragraphs 2 to 8 read through full ResearchGate mirror https://www.researchgate.net/publication/345490244_Beni_Rhenane_Mausolee_Voir_Bourgou_Henchir_Encyclopedie_berbere_fasc_X . Tomb architecture treated as regional royal tradition of disputed date, not Syphax’s personal tomb.

sources.title: CGB Numismatique, Syphax copper coin bgr_336921
sources.note: Primary catalog of an individual coin auctioned in 2014; dimensions, images and legend directly read. CGB’s broad 213 to 200 BCE heading is not used to override historical defeat in 203 BCE. Attribution references Müller 2, CNNM 10, Copenhagen 491 and Alexandropoulos 6.

sources.title: Barclay Head and colleagues, Historia Numorum, second edition (1911), page 887
sources.note: Original numismatic handbook in transcription, directly read. Syphax entry prints the Punic legend in scholarly Hebrew transcription, with Latin Spq. Public sample uses SPQ as confirmed by Lassère and CGB; no claim to have resolved all worn letters on a coin photograph. Historical dates in this old handbook are superseded by modern scholarship.

sources.title: Helma Pasch and François Mbolifouye, Using a Subject Pronoun in Object Position to Claim Power (2011)
sources.note: Original linguistic analysis with Zande consultants in Bangassou. Full public PDF downloaded and read; local zande-pronouns.pdf and text. Pages 2, 4 and 5; example 2 is an accepted form, distinct from debated example 1. Written sample reproduces the researchers’ hyphenated transcription and English translation.

sources.title: Robert O. Collins, A History of Modern Sudan (2008), publisher excerpt
sources.note: Publisher’s indexed full page 8 read; direct PDF access failed. Passage on nineteenth-century movement from Mbomu valley, Gbudwe’s kingdom and killing by a government patrol in 1905. Avoids obsolete pejorative ethnonym and broad linguistic classification.

sources.title: Isaac Waanzi Hillary, On the rebirth of the Azande Kingdom (2024)
sources.note: Original ethnographic research and interviews in Yambio; direct full article read. Nineteenth-century autonomous kingdoms, colonial division, princely appointments, and researcher-witnessed 9 February 2022 modern institution. The 2022 organization is not represented as an independent state or identical restoration.

sources.title: Pitt Rivers Museum, Zande granary, photograph 1998.341.134.2
sources.note: Primary museum record of Evans-Pritchard photograph, Yambio, 1927 to 1930. Full indexed record read. Exact photography year unknown; no invented point metadata.

sources.title: Pitt Rivers Museum, Zande women beating eleusine, photograph 1998.341.427.2
sources.note: Primary photograph catalog, Yambio, 1927 to 1930, full indexed description read. Only direct preparation and porridge/beer uses included, not unqualified nutritional comparison with cassava.

sources.title: Pitt Rivers Museum, Zande potter with pots, photograph 1998.341.320.2
sources.note: Primary photograph catalog and linked observer quotation, Yambio, 1927 to 1930. Full indexed record read. Distinguishes coil-built pots from the adjacent seat; learning joke paraphrases the observer’s admission of failure.

sources.title: Pitt Rivers Museum, Homestead of Zande prince with wives, photograph 1998.341.551.2
sources.note: Primary catalog of photograph specifically dated 1927, household of Rikita, son of Gbudwe. Full indexed record read. Elite household is not generalized to all Zande families.

sources.title: Pitt Rivers Museum, Zande game and stool, photograph 1998.341.317.2
sources.note: Primary photograph catalog, 1927 to 1930, with cross-reference to Schweinfurth’s 1873 account volume 2 page 294. Full indexed record read. No invented rules, number of holes, or claim children alone played.

sources.title: Pitt Rivers Museum, Zande bow harp 1930.86.56
sources.note: Primary artifact documentation, collected 1927 to 1930, made by 1930 rather than definitely in 1930. Full indexed record read; five strings, hide-covered soundbox, wood pegs, plant material.

sources.title: Nicki Kindersley and Yosa Wawa, Rebellious Schooling in a Violent Postcolony (2025)
sources.note: Original archival study, publisher-version indexed page 8 read, journal printed page 457. Wau technical school and Rumba supported by Comboni Archives D556/7 pages 3 to 4. New educational institution explicitly dated after political conquest, no inference that formal schools began all learning.

proposedOverrides.name: Azande
proposedOverrides.summary: Later central African kingdoms, incorrectly placed in a medieval map interval.

batchIdentityNotes.note: Verified eastern Libya geometry and 1715 to 1878 imported interval. Distinct from ancient Cyrene, Tripolitania and later Libya. Public copy explicitly denies a single independent kingdom and treats 1878 as map coverage, not a fall. Hamilton describes an 1852 visit, published 1856; writing sample uses a later Cairo edition of a nineteenth-century author.

Imported interval is 200 to 100 BCE, whereas historical Syphax lost power in 203 BCE. Public overview explicitly exposes mismatch; period uses approximately first attestation around 220 BCE, not a founding date. Border is only an imported general northern African outline; no precise southern boundary asserted. Beni Rhénane date is debated, likely at least partly later; it is regional contextual archaeology, not credited to Syphax. Writing sample deliberately stays in attested scholarly transliteration per root direction.

Verified imported dates 900 to 1000 and outline spanning 16.638 to 42.659 east, 2.491 to 11.956 north; this cannot be treated as documented medieval Zande territory. Narrative explicitly concerns much later states, with period 1800 denoting the start of a nineteenth-century contextual interval, not a founding event. Historical community spans present South Sudan, Central African Republic and Democratic Republic of Congo. Photographic examples mostly dated 1927 to 1930 are explicit colonial-era evidence; 2022 institution described from dated 2024 field study, not as current sovereign state. No original medieval writing claimed.
